entry.title: Rahimi and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2400
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Rahimi’s Class XB Subclass 201 visa under s 501CA(4). Mr Rahimi failed the character test due to a 15-month aggregate sentence, but the Tribunal set aside the delegate’s decision and revoked the cancellation. The case turned on the Direction No 110 balancing, especially mental health, family support and risk of reoffending.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

Federal Court of Australia, 20 Oct 2026, [2026] FCA 1548

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1547
entry.content:
This was a judicial review of the Administrative Review Tribunal’s decision affirming non-revocation of Mr Dabea’s visa cancellation under s 501CA(4) after serious child sexual offences. Mr Dabea alleged the Tribunal failed to properly consider impediments if removed to Fiji and denied procedural fairness by sending post-hearing DFAT country information. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: On judicial review, a tribunal’s reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, so a failure to evaluate a mandatory consideration is not readily inferred merely because the reasons are brief.

The task on judicial review is to read the reasons fairly and as a whole: see EGH19 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 33 at [68] (Gordon, Steward and Gleeson JJ).

entry.title: Application by Crown Melbourne Limited Trading AS Crown Melbourne [2026] FWC 4086
entry.content:
Crown applied under s 229 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for bargaining orders restraining the UWU from alleged misrepresentations during its “vote no” campaign and requiring corrective notices. The Commission considered whether the UWU’s communications and bargaining conduct breached s 228(1)(e) and whether bargaining orders were reasonable. The decision records that orders were not made.

Key holding: A union’s different view of the practical consequences of a proposed agreement is not itself a misrepresentation for good faith bargaining purposes.

That the UWU sees the practical consequences of an effective two-tiered wage system differently to Crown, does not in itself make it a misrepresentation.

entry.title: Application by United Workers' Union (108V) [2026] FWC 4066
entry.content:
The UWU applied for bargaining orders to stop a vote on a proposed Coles subsidiary enterprise agreement, alleging CNSCE had breached the good faith bargaining requirements. The Commission found a breach of s 228(1)(b) for failing to provide the draft agreement in time, but refused the orders because it was not reasonable in all the circumstances. Application dismissed.

Key holding: Timely disclosure of an available draft enterprise agreement is relevant information required by s 228(1)(b); however, a breach does not automatically justify a bargaining order because s 230 requires the Commission to be satisfied an order is reasonable in all the circumstances.

The failure to provide it represents a breach of the good faith bargaining obligations. However, for reasons which are explained below, including the UWU's own failure to present bargaining proposals, and failure to identify any issues it had adverted to with the proposed agreement after it received a copy of it ( on 8 October 2026), weigh against it being reasonable in all circumstances to make the orders sought.

entry.title: Application by Mrs Marietna Di Marcantonio [2026] FWC 4081
entry.content:
Mrs Di Marcantonio applied under s 789FC of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an order to stop bullying against her former employer and three named individuals. After her employment ended, the Commission considered whether the application should be dismissed because there was no continuing risk of bullying. Deputy President Butler dismissed the application under s 587(1)(c).

Key holding: Where an applicant no longer works with the named persons and there is no foreseeable risk of return, the Commission lacks jurisdiction to make stop-bullying orders and the application has no reasonable prospects of success.

In the absence of any continuing risk and having regard to my consideration above, there is no jurisdiction to make an order to stop bullying. Therefore, the application has no reasonable prospects of success.

entry.title: The Civil Air Operations Officers’ Association Of Australia Trading AS Civil Air v Airservices Australia [2026] FWC 3820
entry.content:
Civil Air applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to arbitrate a dispute about redundancy-type benefits under the Airservices Australia (Air Traffic Control and Supporting Air Traffic Services) Enterprise Agreement 2024-2027. The dispute concerned whether air traffic controllers who cannot obtain, or refuse to obtain, a National Security Clearance or Citizenship Eligibility Waiver are entitled to cl 62.13(a)(i)-(ii) benefits on termination.

Key holding: Clause 62.13 termination benefits require the employee to be a “potentially surplus employee” under cl 62.2, and inability or refusal to obtain an NSC or CEW does not make an ATC surplus where the class of ATCs remains required.

For these reasons I do not consider that employees who are unable or refuse to obtain an NSC (or CEW) can qualify for the entitlements in clause 62.13(a)(i) and (ii) because they are in a class of employees formally identified by the Respondent as a class which has a greater number of employees in it that is necessary for its efficient and economical working, within the meaning of clause 62.2(a) of the Agreement.

entry.title: CMTWN and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2399
entry.content:
In CMTWN and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2399, the applicant sought review of an NDIA decision dated 27 May 2026 concerning NDIS plan variations. The Tribunal found the application did not seek review of an internal review decision under s 100(6) of the NDIS Act when filed and was premature. It dismissed the application under s 97 of the ART Act and held it had no power to treat the submissions as a new application.

Key holding: Where an application does not seek review of a reviewable decision, the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction and must dismiss it under s 97 of the ART Act.

The Tribunal must dismiss an application if: (a) the application is made for review of a decision; and (b) the Tribunal is satisfied that the decision is not reviewable by the Tribunal.

entry.title: Xi and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2397
entry.content:
The applicant, a Chinese national, had his Resident Return (Class BB) (Subclass 155) visa mandatorily cancelled under s 501(3A) after being sentenced to 48 months’ imprisonment for offences arising from a cybercrime scam syndicate and firearm possession. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation under s 501CA(4), and the Tribunal affirmed that decision. The Tribunal found the offending serious and that community protection and expectations outweighed a low risk of reoffending and the applicant’s ties.

Key holding: Serious offending may cause the community expectations consideration under Direction No 110 to weigh significantly against revocation despite an applicant’s personal circumstances.

In the present case, the Tribunal has found the applicant's offending is serious. Taking into consideration the personal circumstances of the applicant, it considers this consideration weighs significantly against revocation of the cancellation.

entry.title: Hoang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2396
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed the Minister’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Hoang’s Class BF Transitional (Permanent) visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although Mr Hoang had a substantial criminal record for repeat drug and weapons offending and failed the character test, the Tribunal found another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4) and set aside the refusal.

Key holding: A residual risk of reoffending may be acceptable, and another reason to revoke may exist, where serious addiction-related offending is offset by sustained rehabilitation, family support and long residence.

The Applicant has, nonetheless, made significant progress in rehabilitation and has retained the support and trust of his immediate family who are an important element to his future success. I consider that the 'residual' risk of reoffending is acceptable despite the potentially serious consequences for the community, and Mr Hoang's length of residence from a young age must take into account.

entry.title: Sarah Mcinnes v Le Luxe Design & Construct Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4064
entry.content:
Ms McInnes filed an unfair dismissal application on 20 August 2026, 87 days after her employment was said to have ended on 25 May 2026, outside the 21-day statutory period. The Fair Work Commission was not satisfied there were exceptional circumstances and dismissed the extension application.

Key holding: Under s 394(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist before extending time for an unfair dismissal application, regardless of the length of delay.

Regardless of the length of the delay, where an application is lodged outside the statutory time limit, the Commission must be satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances supporting an extension of time.

entry.title: Michiaki Miyazaki v Sydney Omakase Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3383
entry.content:
Miyazaki v Sydney Omakase Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3383 concerned an unfair dismissal claim by a Head Chef dismissed for alleged drinking at work. The Fair Work Commission found the employer’s summary dismissal was not consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code and that the dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable. Compensation was awarded.

Key holding: A dismissal is not consistent with the Summary Dismissal limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code where the employer’s actual reason is a performance concern rather than a belief, held on reasonable grounds at dismissal, that the employee’s conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal.

I do not accept that Mr Best, on behalf of Sydney Omakase, held a belief that Mr Miyazaki's conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal. This is because I find that the reason for dismissal, based on Mr Best's witness statement, was that Mr Miyazaki was unable to confirm that he had the passion to continue as Head Chef.

entry.title: Kacy Brazier v OS MCAP Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4043
entry.content:
This Fair Work Commission decision concerns an order for lost pay following an earlier finding that Kacy Brazier was unfairly dismissed and an order for his reinstatement. The Commission awarded reduced lost pay under s 391 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) because Brazier made no real attempt to find paid work for most of his unemployment and performed unpaid work for his then partner. The total compensation ordered was $98,965.03 gross less tax plus $11,875.80 superannuation.

Key holding: An order to restore lost pay is discretionary and a deliberate failure to mitigate loss may reduce or defeat any award.

It cannot be said that he was unsophisticated or unaware that a deliberate failure to mitigate his loss would affect any award of lost pay at the Commission's discretion.

entry.title: Application by Transport Workers' Union of Australia (179V) [2026] FWC 4051
entry.content:
Deputy President Hampton determined a s.437 protected action ballot order application by the TWU for Cleanaway employees covered by three regional Victorian waste enterprise agreements. The employer objected to scope and ballot questions 5, 9 and 10, including safety-related wording; the Commission rejected the continuing objections and granted the application, with leave to amend some questions. The ballot will be run by Fair Vote Services Pty Ltd and close on 5 November 2026.

Key holding: Under s.443(1) and (3)(d), where a valid s.437 application proposes clear ballot questions, the Commission must make a PABO and has no general discretion to exclude valid questions or amend them merely due to employer objections to wording.

The inference to be drawn from the mandatory nature of s 443(1) is that the order required to be made is one which gives effect to an application validly made under s 437. Thus, in respect of s 443(3)(d), we do not consider that the Commission has a general discretion to determine the questions which will be included in the order, or to simply exclude valid questions, independent of what has been applied for.

entry.title: Application by Southern Cross Care [2026] FWC 4067
entry.content:
Southern Cross Care (Qld) Ltd sought orders under s 318(1)(a) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to displace the Broken Hill Agreement for transferring Oasis employees and replace it with Queensland enterprise agreements. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application after weighing the s 318(3) considerations. Employee disadvantage and the public interest weighed against the transfer.

Key holding: The Commission may decline orders under s 318(1)(a) where the mandatory s 318(3) considerations, especially employee disadvantage and the public interest, weigh against the transfer.

On a whole, taking into account the mandatory considerations under s 318(3), I do not consider it appropriate to exercise my discretion to make the orders sought. Particularly, I consider the disadvantage to the employees and public interest are matters which should be given more weight in this application, and which weigh against the orders sought.

entry.title: Roberto Biguzzi v Eco Alliance Pty. Ltd. [2026] FWC 3872
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with an unfair dismissal application by a former Senior Sales Representative whose role was made redundant after the employer closed its internal sales function. The employer asserted genuine redundancy under s 389, but the Commission found the job was no longer required due operational requirements while the written consultation did not satisfy cl 27.2 of the Miscellaneous Award 2020. The provided extract does not include final orders on the remaining s 387 merits.

Key holding: For a genuine redundancy defence under s 389(1)(b), written consultation must explain the nature of the major change itself, not merely its effects or causes.

It would in my view be insufficient to meet the written notice requirements in clause 27.2 to deal only with the effects of the changes without explaining what the changes actually are. This is consistent with "nature" and "effect" being separately itemised in paragraphs (a) and (b) of clause 27.2.

entry.title: Peter Andrew Staas v Assta Labels Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4050
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair dismissal application by Peter Staas against his family company employer, Assta Labels Pty Ltd, under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Mr Staas was dismissed after repeatedly refusing to attend an independent medical examination, and the Commission found there was a valid reason and procedural fairness, dismissing the application.

Key holding: A direction to attend an independent medical examination can be lawful and reasonable—and refusal can supply a valid reason for dismissal—where the employee’s health is causally linked to ongoing performance concerns and the employer seeks to assess capacity and possible adjustments.

I am satisfied that the direction to attend an independent medical examination was lawful and reasonable each time a direction was given to Peter in the last four months of his employment. Peter 's refusal to follow this lawful and reasonable direction was a valid reason to dismiss him from his employment with Assta Labels.

entry.title: Mr Muhammad Ahsan Malik v On The Run Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4054
entry.content:
Mr Malik filed an unfair dismissal application 23 days after the 21-day statutory period expired. The Commission refused an extension because he had no satisfactory explanation for the delay, knew of the dismissal immediately, and the remaining factors were neutral or only marginally supportive. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: In weighing the s 394(3) factors, a marginal favour from the applicant’s efforts to dispute dismissal is outweighed by the lack of a satisfactory reason for delay and immediate awareness of dismissal, so no exceptional circumstances are established.

Balancing the factor that weighs marginally in favour of a finding of exceptional circumstances, being the Applicant's efforts to dispute his dismissal, against the factors weighing more heavily against such a finding, being the lack of a satisfactory reason for delay and the Applicant's awareness of the dismissal on the day it was conveyed by the Respondent, I find that there are no exceptional circumstances in this matter.

entry.title: Dane Harris v Wr Timbers Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4061
entry.content:
Mr Harris applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after WR Timbers Pty Ltd made his full-time Manager position redundant. The Fair Work Commission upheld the employer’s genuine redundancy objection under s.389 and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A dismissal is a genuine redundancy where the employer establishes the s.389(1) matters and that reasonable redeployment was not available in all the circumstances under s.389(2).

I am satisfied that the Respondent has satisfied the requirements of s.389(1) and (2) of the Act. The dismissal of Mr Harris is a genuine redundancy.

entry.title: Delaney King v Advanced Mobile IT Pty Limited [2026] FWC 4047
entry.content:
Ms King applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after AMIT made her part-time finance/administrative role redundant in March 2026. The Commission had to decide whether the dismissal was a genuine redundancy under s 389, so that it was not unfair under s 385.

Key holding: A dismissal is a genuine redundancy only if all three limbs of s 389 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) are established: operational change removing the need for the job, consultation compliance, and no reasonable redeployment.

All three limbs of s 389 must be established for a dismissal to be a genuine redundancy.

entry.title: Mr David Peter Grant v Metric PCM [2026] FWC 3937
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered whether David Grant’s dismissal by Metric PCM Pty Ltd was a genuine redundancy after the EDL Energy contract ended. It found all three elements of genuine redundancy under s 389 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) were satisfied, notwithstanding informal consultation and temporary alternative duties. Metric PCM’s jurisdictional objection was upheld and Mr Grant’s unfair dismissal application was dismissed.

Key holding: A dismissal meeting the s 389 definition of genuine redundancy cannot be an unfair dismissal because the person cannot satisfy the definition in s 385.

Given my three findings above, Mr Grant's dismissal was a case of "genuine redundancy" as defined in s.389 of the FW Act. That means Mr Grant cannot satisfy the definition of an unfair dismissal in s.385 of the FW Act.

entry.title: Barresi v Cross Yarra Partnerships [2026] VSC 666
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a second Wrongs Act Medical Panel determination that his whole person impairment did not meet the threshold, after an earlier panel had found that it did. The Court followed Citywide Service Solutions Pty Ltd v Rosata in permitting the later panel to determine the same medical question, and rejected the challenge based on s 28LZG(4). The catchwords record “Appeal dismissed”.

Key holding: An asserted misunderstanding by a Medical Panel of s 28LZG(4) will not constitute jurisdictional error unless the misunderstanding was material to the determination, in the sense that the decision could realistically have been different.

Consequently, in my opinion, the plaintiff has not established that the asserted misunderstanding by the second Panel of s 28LZG(4) was material to the decision that the second Panel made and therefore jurisdictional error has not been established.

entry.title: FWKPM and Chief Executive Officer, National Insurance Disability Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2402
entry.content:

A Registrar refused the requests on excessive-scope and privacy grounds, but the Tribunal held the documents were apparently relevant and privacy did not justify refusal. The Tribunal issued all three summonses with a return date of 30 October 2026.

Key holding: Where documents are of apparent relevance and no party objects, the Tribunal should ordinarily exercise its discretion to issue a summons unless the summons is vexatious, frivolous or otherwise an abuse of process.

I would add one further observation, namely that generally speaking where a party asks for a summons, the documents sought are of apparent relevance, and no other party objects to the summons being issued, the discretion to issue a summons should ordinarily be exercised, unless it vexatious or frivolous or otherwise an abuse of process to issue the summons.

entry.title: WNZP and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2398
entry.content:
This was a second review in a child support matter concerning the parents’ percentage of care for two children after the Mother notified a change of care on 23 March 2024. The Tribunal recalculated actual care, rejected an argument that the Father’s overseas absences meant he had relinquished care, and declined to record court-ordered care under s 51 because the change predated 29 March 2024. The decision under review was set aside and new care percentages were substituted.

Key holding: Under the law applying before 29 March 2024, an interim care determination under s 51 cannot be made where existing care percentages are revoked under s 54F or s 54H.

I am bound by the Court's interpretation in CMU23 and must apply the legislation in force prior to 29 March 2024, specifically paragraph 53(1)(c), such that an interim determination cannot be made when existing percentages of care are revoked either pursuant to section 54F or section 54H of the Act.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.

Key holding: When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

entry.title: Foong v Health Care Complaints Commission [2026] NSWCA 217
entry.content:
Dr Andrew Foong sought leave to appeal from NCAT’s refusal to recuse Principal Member Ainslie-Wallace AM ADCJ in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Health Care Complaints Commission. This attitude had no potential to have any effect in the present proceedings as Dr Kertesz's expertise as a general practitioner was accepted.

The Tribunal adjourned the hearing to allow the Respondent time to consider the late additions and, under s 53 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), fixed the issues in dispute. No final merits decision on the NDIS supports was made.

Key holding: The Tribunal may determine the scope of review by limiting the questions of fact, evidence and issues it considers.

In a proceeding for review of a decision, the Tribunal may determine the scope of the review by limiting the questions of fact, the evidence and the issues that it considers.

entry.title: Mishra and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2327
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Mishra’s Subclass 155 Five-Year Resident Return visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Mr Mishra accepted he did not pass the character test because of a 22-month aggregate sentence for family violence offences. The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision after considering whether another reason existed under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) and Direction No. 110.

Key holding: Where a visa is mandatorily cancelled because the holder fails the character test due to a substantial criminal record, the Tribunal must consider whether there is another reason to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No. 110.

In accordance with s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), the Tribunal must therefore consider whether there is another reason to exercise the discretion under s 501CA(4) to revoke the original decision.

entry.title: Onyema v Commonwealth of Australia (as represented by the Australian Taxation Office) (extension of time, application for stay) [2026] FCA 1530
entry.content:
Kenneth Onyema sought judicial review of the ATO’s decision to terminate his APS employment for unauthorised access to taxation records. In this interlocutory judgment, the Federal Court held that he did not need an extension of time, refused a stay of the termination decision, granted leave to amend, and fixed the proper respondents.

Key holding: Under s 11(1)(c) of the ADJR Act, an application for review is “lodged” when it comes into the possession of the Registry or its staff, not when it is later accepted and filed, so receipt within the prescribed period satisfies the time limit.

An application for review will be "lodged" when it comes into the possession of a Registry or a staff of a Registry: EIW20 at [67], quoting Hong v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [1998] FCA 341; (1998) 82 FCR 468 at 471 (the Court).
